starlink: SpaceX's Starlink is a low-Earth orbit broadband constellation designed to provide internet access worldwide through a network of satellites and ground stations.  Unlike the legacy players in satellite IoT technology from the late 1990s/early 2000s (e.g., Iridium, Globalstar, Orbcomm), Starlink operates at much lower altitudes to reduce latency and increase bandwidth.  While advantageous for internet connectivity, the low operating altitude and unprecedented scale of the constellation requires strict space traffic management to avoid collisions and mitigate space debris.
amazonleo: Amazon Leo, formerly Project Kuiper, is Amazon's low-Earth orbit broadband constellation intended to provide high-speed internet connectivity.  One of Amazon Leo's competitive features is its ability to integrate directly into Amazon Web Services (AWS), thereby turning its satellites into a private, space-based extension of a company's cloud network and allowing data to travel from remote locations straight into AWS servers without ever touching the public internet.
guowang: Guowang, translated from Mandarin to the "National Network" constellation, is China's state-sponsored low-Earth orbit broadband constellation intended to provide global communications coverage.
qianfan: Qianfan, translated from Mandarin to the "Thousand Sails" constellation, is a Chinese broadband satellite network backed by a combination of military and state funding.
oneweb: Eutelsat OneWeb is a low-Earth orbit communications constellation providing broadband connectivity to enterprise, government, and remote users. Founded in 2012, the company survived a 2020 bankruptcy through a UK government-backed rescue and merged with French satellite giant Eutelsat in 2023, which is now actively launching Airbus-built replacement satellites to refresh its aging first-generation fleet.
starshield: SpaceX Starshield is a government-focused satellite program derived from Starlink technology, supporting U.S. national security and other government missions.
pwsa: The Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture is a U.S. Space Force program deploying networked low-Earth orbit satellites for military communications and missile warning and tracking.
jilin: Jilin-1 (named after the Jilin province in northeastern China) is China's largest commercial Earth-observation satellite network that captures sub-meter imagery and 4K full-color video from space. Rather than providing internet or phone service, it takes rapid, high-resolution pictures for agriculture, disaster response, urban planning, etc. Jilin-1 has also drawn geopolitical scrutiny (and U.S. sanctions) for its ability to track moving military vehicles and aircraft in near-real time.
spire: Spire Global operates a nanosatellite constellation focused on radio-frequency sensing, including weather observations, maritime tracking, and aviation data. The majority of Spire's satellites are Low Earth Multi-Use Receiver 2 (LEMUR-2) 3U CubeSats, which generate large amounts of Earth and space science data (which agencies like NASA, NOAA, and ESA purchase for research and forecasting) alongside tracking global shipping and air traffic.
planet: Planet operates its many "flocks" of "Dove" 3U CubeSats with the goal of imaging the Earth's entire landmass every single day to make global change visible and actionable for agriculture, disaster response, environmental monitoring, etc.
iridium: Originating as one of the legacy players in satellite internet in the mid 1990s, the modern Iridium constellation is a global network of 66 active satellites (plus some in-active spares) operating in low-Earth orbit delivering pole-to-pole voice/data communications for aviation, maritime, and defense users. While the modern architecture was streamlined to 66 active satellites, it was originaly designed for 77 satellites, leading to its namesake of the element iridium (atomic number 77).  The network is set to be acquired by Rocket Lab in mid-2027.
globalstar: The Globalstar constellation, originally launched in the late 1990s alongside Iridium and Orbcommm, is a legacy low-Earth orbit satellite network that provides mobile voice, data, and IoT connectivity.  Today, the network is best known for powering Apple's Emergency SOS and off-grid satellite messaging features on iPhone 14 and newer models, and it is set to be acquired by Amazon to bolster its direct-to-device satellite ambitions.
orbcomm: The Orbcomm constellation is a legacy low-Earth orbit satellite network launched in the late 1990s alongside Iridium and Globalstar.  Orbcomm specializes in low-bandwidth machine-to-machine (M2M) data and industrial IoT asset tracking rather than voice calls. Taken private by GI Partners in 2021, the company sold its maritime vessel-tracking (Automatic Identification System, or AIS) unit to S&P Global in late 2025 while continuing to operate its core fleet and cargo monitoring network.
strela1m: The Strela-1M constellation was a Cold War-era Soviet military communications network comprised of hundreds of tiny, disposable 60-kilogram satellites. Rather than streaming live calls, each satellite acted as an orbiting mailbox that recorded messages from Soviet military units on the ground and replayed them later when passing over home territory. Designed with a roughly six-month lifespan and no onboard propulsion, the network relied on sheer numbers and regular replacement launches, leaving behind hundreds of defunct satellites that will remain in orbit as space debris for centuries.
strela3: The Strela-3 and Strela-3M constellations are the second- and third-generation successors to the Cold War-era Strela-1M military network, upgrading 1M's tiny, disposable six-month satellites into longer-lasting orbiting mailboxes. Launched starting in 1985, Strela-3 satellites are designed to last five years, store encrypted bursts from intelligence agents' portable radios, and "dump"them over Russian ground stations. Since 2005, Russia has transitioned the system to the modernized Strela-3M (Rodnik) series.
